abstract: Urbanization can alter dietary stoichiometry by changing the elemental composition of food resources or the mixture of resources consumers assimilate. However, the relative contributions of resource elemental quality and assimilated diet composition to dietary stoichiometry, and whether the resulting dietary differences are reflected in consumer body stoichiometry, remain poorly understood, particularly in omnivores. We sampled adult female Trinidadian guppies (Poecilia reticulata) and their food resources from paired high-urbanization (HU) and low-urbanization (LU) sites in three rivers of Trinidad's Northern Range. Combining hierarchical Bayesian stable-isotope mixing models with resource %C, %N, and %P, we reconstructed dietary stoichiometry, partitioned differences between urbanization levels into contributions from diet composition and resource elemental quality, and compared these with somatic stoichiometry. Under the primary mixing model, aquatic invertebrates contributed less to estimated HU diets (33.7 percentage points lower; 95% credible interval [5.0, 60.1]), whereas detrital contributions tended to be higher. Resource elemental composition showed no consistent differences between urbanization levels. Under this model, reconstructed dietary N:P ratios were lower in HU guppies (by 59.2% [10.0, 81.8]), while C:N ratios tended to be higher, and C:P ratios tended to be lower. Changes in assimilated source mixtures contributed more strongly than resource elemental quality to C:N and N:P differences. All of these contrasts depended on the estimated trophic discrimination factors, weakening under fixed literature values, with the C:N contrast reversing under two of them and the detrital contrast varying in direction. Guppy somatic tissues partly tracked these dietary differences. HU guppies tended to have lower somatic C:P and N:P ratios, in the same direction as their diets but of smaller magnitude. Somatic C:N showed no clear difference, and the dietary C:N contrast was itself uncertain. Our findings suggest that urbanization reshapes guppy dietary stoichiometry mainly through shifts in which resources they assimilate, and that guppies only partially pass these shifts into their bodies. Understanding the stoichiometric consequences of environmental change therefore requires considering not only what resources contain, but also which resources consumers assimilate.
